# Question 2(c) and 2(d): Clustering the Households {#sec-cluster}

## Choosing the method

The clustering method used is **agglomerative hierarchical clustering**. It works from the bottom up: each household starts as its own cluster, and at each step the two most similar clusters are combined into a bigger cluster until all households belong to one cluster. Unlike k-means, hierarchical clustering does not need the number of clusters to be fixed in advance, and its results can be shown as a dendrogram, which helps in deciding the final number of clusters.

The dissimilarity between households is measured with the **Euclidean distance**, the most commonly used distance measure. Euclidean distance needs numeric variables on a similar scale and is sensitive to outliers. These requirements were met in @sec-prep, where the six variables were skew-corrected and standardised so that no variable dominates the distance because of its larger range of values.

The linkage method is **Ward's minimum variance method** [@ward1963]. At each step it merges the pair of clusters whose merger gives the **smallest increase in the total within-cluster sum of squares**, so it tends to produce compact clusters of similar size. For agglomerative clustering, complete linkage and Ward's method are often preferred. Single linkage was not used because it tends to chain households into long, loose clusters.

## Choosing the number of groups {#sec-choose-k}

```{r}
#| label: choose-k
#| fig-width: 10
#| fig-height: 4

# Cluster on the six variables only (MemberID is a label, not behaviour)
cluster_data <- soap_prep |> select(all_of(cluster_vars))

# Elbow and silhouette using hierarchical clustering with Ward's linkage
p_elbow <- fviz_nbclust(cluster_data, FUNcluster = hcut, method = "wss",
                        k.max = 10, hc_method = "ward.D2") +
  labs(title = "(A) Elbow method")

p_silhouette <- fviz_nbclust(cluster_data, FUNcluster = hcut, method = "silhouette",
                             k.max = 10, hc_method = "ward.D2") +
  labs(title = "(B) Silhouette method")

p_elbow + p_silhouette
```

```{r}
#| label: ward-tree
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 4.5

# Hierarchical clustering: Euclidean distance, Ward's linkage
distance_ward <- dist(cluster_data, method = "euclidean")
hc_ward <- hclust(distance_ward, method = "ward.D2")

# Number of clusters selected (justified below)
k_final <- 6

# The dendrogram cut into k_final groups, coloured with the team palette
fviz_dend(hc_ward, k = k_final, show_labels = FALSE, k_colors = pal[1:k_final],
          main = "Dendrogram (Ward's linkage), cut into six groups")
```

```{r}
#| label: tbl-k-compare
#| tbl-cap: "Candidate numbers of groups compared: group sizes and average silhouette width."

# For each k, cut the Ward tree and record group sizes and average silhouette width
k_compare <- tibble(k = 2:6) |>
  mutate(groups = map(k, \(kk) cutree(hc_ward, k = kk)),
         sizes = map_chr(groups, \(g) paste(table(g), collapse = ", ")),
         smallest = map_int(groups, \(g) min(table(g))),
         average_silhouette = map_dbl(groups, \(g) mean(silhouette(g, distance_ward)[, "sil_width"])))

k_compare |>
  select(-groups) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(average_silhouette, decimals = 3) |>
  cols_label(k = "Groups (k)", sizes = "Households per group",
             smallest = "Smallest group", average_silhouette = "Average silhouette")
```

```{r}
#| label: k-values
#| echo: false

sil <- \(kk) sprintf("%.3f", k_compare$average_silhouette[k_compare$k == kk])
sizes_of <- \(kk) sort(table(cutree(hc_ward, k = kk)), decreasing = TRUE)
k2 <- sizes_of(2)
# The group of five that is split in two when moving to six
split_parent <- max(table(cutree(hc_ward, k = 5)))
split_kids   <- setdiff(as.integer(table(cutree(hc_ward, k = 6))), as.integer(table(cutree(hc_ward, k = 5))))
smallest6    <- min(table(cutree(hc_ward, k = 6)))
```

The elbow and silhouette methods do not agree on a clear number of clusters. The silhouette method favours two clusters, where the average silhouette width peaks at `r sil(2)`, and it falls sharply at three. However, six clusters are a close second at `r sil(6)`, above three, four and five clusters (`r sil(3)`, `r sil(4)` and `r sil(5)`). All silhouette values [@rousseeuw1987] are close to 0, which means many households lie near the border between clusters: the groups overlap rather than being sharply separated. The elbow plot does not give a clear answer either, as the largest drop is from one to two clusters and the curve flattens out after six.

**Six clusters were chosen because the clusters also need to make business sense.** The aim of the segmentation is to help XYZ's clients run several promotions, each aimed at a different segment, and to design reward schemes that build brand loyalty. Six segments is a manageable number of separate campaigns for a client to run across a year, and each segment needs a different approach: reward schemes suit loyal households, while households that buy on promotion respond to discounts. With two clusters, the Heavy multi-brand shoppers and the Promo-6 buyers form one cluster of `r k2[2]` households and everyone else forms a second cluster of `r k2[1]`. That would combine households that buy very differently, such as loyal buyers and light occasional buyers. Moving from five to six clusters splits the largest group of `r split_parent` households into `r max(split_kids)` loyal households that rarely buy on promotion and `r min(split_kids)` loyal households that buy heavily on other promotions. These behave differently and call for different promotions. More clusters would risk very small groups, but with six the smallest still holds `r smallest6` households (`r percent(smallest6 / nrow(soap_prep), accuracy = 1)` of the panel).

## The final grouping

```{r}
#| label: final-clusters

# Cut the Ward tree into k_final groups
ward_groups <- cutree(hc_ward, k = k_final)

# Names chosen from the standardised group means (see the centroid chart below)
segment_names <- c("1" = "Mainstream non-loyal buyers",
                   "2" = "Heavy multi-brand shoppers",
                   "3" = "Light occasional buyers",
                   "4" = "Loyal regular-price buyers",
                   "5" = "Loyal promotion buyers",
                   "6" = "Promo-6 buyers")

# Each household's cluster and segment name, used for profiling (2e) and PCA (Q3)
soap_clusters <- tibble(MemberID = soap_prep$MemberID,
                        cluster  = factor(ward_groups)) |>
  mutate(segment = unname(segment_names[as.character(cluster)]))
```

Cutting the Ward dendrogram into six clusters gives segments of `r min(table(ward_groups))` to `r max(table(ward_groups))` households. Each segment was given a label based on its average values on the six variables, and each household's cluster and segment name are stored in `soap_clusters` for the rest of the analysis.

### Does the result depend on the method?

To check whether the segments depend on the clustering method, k-means was also run with six clusters. K-means assigns each household to the cluster with the nearest centroid, recalculates each centroid as the mean of its cluster, and repeats until the assignments stop changing. Because the starting centroids are random, k-means was run with 25 random starts, keeping the solution with the lowest total within-cluster variation, and the seed is set right before it so the result repeats exactly.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-ward-vs-kmeans
#| tbl-cap: "Cross table of the Ward segments (rows) against the k-means groups (columns)."

set.seed(55789)   # k-means uses random starting centroids
km_check <- kmeans(cluster_data, centers = k_final, nstart = 25)

ward_vs_km <- table(Ward = ward_groups, Kmeans = km_check$cluster)

# k-means numbers its groups differently, so agreement is read from the largest
# count in each row: the share of households in their best-matching k-means group
agreement     <- sum(apply(ward_vs_km, 1, max)) / length(ward_groups)
row_agreement <- apply(ward_vs_km, 1, max) / rowSums(ward_vs_km)

as.data.frame.matrix(ward_vs_km) |>
  as_tibble(rownames = "cluster") |>
  mutate(segment = segment_names[cluster], agreement = row_agreement) |>
  select(segment, everything(), -cluster) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_percent(agreement, decimals = 0) |>
  tab_spanner(label = "k-means group", columns = as.character(1:k_final)) |>
  cols_label(segment = "Ward segment", agreement = "In best-matching group")
```

```{r}
#| label: kmeans-stability

# Repeat k-means 10 times with different random starts: does the agreement hold?
stability_runs <- map_dbl(1:10, \(i) {
  km  <- kmeans(cluster_data, centers = k_final, nstart = 25)
  tab <- table(ward_groups, km$cluster)
  sum(apply(tab, 1, max)) / length(ward_groups)
})
range(stability_runs)
```

```{r}
#| label: kmeans-values
#| echo: false

ra <- \(seg) percent(row_agreement[names(segment_names)[segment_names == seg]], accuracy = 1)
```

Overall, `r percent(agreement, accuracy = 0.1)` of households sit in their best-matching k-means group. Agreement is highest for the Light occasional buyers (`r ra("Light occasional buyers")`) and the Promo-6 buyers (`r ra("Promo-6 buyers")`), followed by the Loyal promotion buyers (`r ra("Loyal promotion buyers")`), the Loyal regular-price buyers (`r ra("Loyal regular-price buyers")`) and the Heavy multi-brand shoppers (`r ra("Heavy multi-brand shoppers")`). It is lowest for the Mainstream non-loyal buyers (`r ra("Mainstream non-loyal buyers")`), whose households are split across several k-means groups. This moderate agreement is consistent with the low silhouette values in @sec-choose-k: many households lie close to the border between clusters, and the "average" segment is the least sharply defined. Repeating k-means ten times with different random starts gave almost the same agreement each time (`r percent(min(stability_runs), accuracy = 0.1)` to `r percent(max(stability_runs), accuracy = 0.1)`), so the comparison does not depend on one particular set of starting centroids.

## Describing each group (2d)

```{r}
#| label: tbl-segment-means
#| tbl-cap: "How each segment buys bath soap, in original units, with the all-household average in the last row."

# Attach each household's segment to its original (untransformed) values
original_segment <- soap_clusters |>
  left_join(soap_clean |> select(MemberID, all_of(cluster_vars)), by = "MemberID")

# Group sizes and means, plus an all-households row for comparison
segment_means <- original_segment |>
  group_by(cluster, segment) |>
  summarise(households = n(), across(all_of(cluster_vars), mean), .groups = "drop") |>
  bind_rows(original_segment |>
              summarise(households = n(), across(all_of(cluster_vars), mean)) |>
              mutate(segment = "All households"))

segment_means |>
  select(-cluster) |>
  gt() |>
  fmt_number(c(TotalVol, NoTrans, NoBrands), decimals = 1) |>
  fmt_percent(c(PurPromo6, PurOtherPromo, MaxBrShare), decimals = 0) |>
  cols_label(segment = "Segment", households = "Households",
             TotalVol = "Total volume", NoTrans = "Transactions",
             PurPromo6 = "Share on promo 6", PurOtherPromo = "Share on other promos",
             NoBrands = "Brands bought", MaxBrShare = "Share to top brand") |>
  tab_style(style = cell_text(weight = "bold"),
            locations = cells_body(rows = segment == "All households"))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-centroids
#| fig-cap: "Segment centroids: the mean of each standardised variable within each segment (0 = the average household)."
#| fig-width: 9
#| fig-height: 7

soap_prep |>
  left_join(soap_clusters, by = "MemberID") |>
  group_by(segment) |>
  summarise(across(all_of(cluster_vars), mean)) |>
  pivot_longer(-segment, names_to = "variable", values_to = "mean_z") |>
  mutate(segment  = factor(segment, levels = segment_names),
         variable = factor(variable, levels = rev(cluster_vars))) |>
  ggplot(aes(mean_z, variable, fill = mean_z > 0)) +
  geom_col(show.legend = FALSE) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = 0, colour = "grey40") +
  facet_wrap(~segment, ncol = 2) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c(`TRUE` = pal[1], `FALSE` = pal[4])) +
  labs(title = "Segment centroids on the six purchase variables",
       x = "Standardised mean (0 = average household)", y = NULL)
```

```{r}
#| label: segment-values
#| echo: false

# Look-ups for the paragraphs below, so every number comes from the table above
sm  <- \(seg, col) segment_means[[col]][segment_means$segment == seg]
avg <- \(col) sm("All households", col)
n_  <- \(seg) sm(seg, "households")
p_  <- \(x) percent(x, accuracy = 1)
v_  <- \(x) comma(x, accuracy = 100)
```

@tbl-segment-means gives each segment's size and average purchase behaviour in original units, with the average for all households in the last row. @fig-centroids shows the same segments on the standardised scale: bars to the right are above the average household and bars to the left are below it, so the longest bars show what makes each segment distinctive.

**Mainstream non-loyal buyers** (`r n_("Mainstream non-loyal buyers")` households, `r p_(n_("Mainstream non-loyal buyers") / 600)` of the panel). These households buy close to the average amount of soap, about `r v_(sm("Mainstream non-loyal buyers", "TotalVol"))` units over `r round(sm("Mainstream non-loyal buyers", "NoTrans"))` transactions, and rarely buy on promotion (`r p_(sm("Mainstream non-loyal buyers", "PurPromo6"))` of volume on promotion 6 and `r p_(sm("Mainstream non-loyal buyers", "PurOtherPromo"))` on other promotions). Only `r p_(sm("Mainstream non-loyal buyers", "MaxBrShare"))` of their volume goes to their top named brand, well below the average of `r p_(avg("MaxBrShare"))`, so this segment is not loyal to any named brand. Because they rarely buy on promotion, discounts are unlikely to change their habits.

**Heavy multi-brand shoppers** (`r n_("Heavy multi-brand shoppers")` households, `r p_(n_("Heavy multi-brand shoppers") / 600)`). This segment buys the most soap, about `r v_(sm("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "TotalVol"))` units, which is `r p_(sm("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "TotalVol") / avg("TotalVol") - 1)` more than the average household, and buys most often, with about `r round(sm("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "NoTrans"))` transactions against an average of `r round(avg("NoTrans"))`. They spread their volume over the most brands (`r round(sm("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "NoBrands"), 1)` on average against `r round(avg("NoBrands"), 1)` overall) with only `r p_(sm("Heavy multi-brand shoppers", "MaxBrShare"))` going to their top brand. Their volume is large but divided between brands, so reward schemes that encourage them to keep buying the same brand suit this segment.

**Light occasional buyers** (`r n_("Light occasional buyers")` households, `r p_(n_("Light occasional buyers") / 600)`). These households buy very little, about `r v_(sm("Light occasional buyers", "TotalVol"))` units over only `r round(sm("Light occasional buyers", "NoTrans"), 1)` transactions, roughly a ninth of the average volume. They did not buy on promotion at all and bought the fewest brands (`r round(sm("Light occasional buyers", "NoBrands"), 1)` against `r round(avg("NoBrands"), 1)`). Given their small volume they should be a low priority for promotion spending.

**Loyal regular-price buyers** (`r n_("Loyal regular-price buyers")` households, `r p_(n_("Loyal regular-price buyers") / 600)`). These households buy slightly more than average, about `r v_(sm("Loyal regular-price buyers", "TotalVol"))` units, in fewer transactions (`r round(sm("Loyal regular-price buyers", "NoTrans"))` against `r round(avg("NoTrans"))`). They give `r p_(sm("Loyal regular-price buyers", "MaxBrShare"))` of their volume to one brand and almost never buy on promotion (`r p_(sm("Loyal regular-price buyers", "PurPromo6"))` on promotion 6 and `r p_(sm("Loyal regular-price buyers", "PurOtherPromo"))` on others). Since they already buy their favourite brand without discounts, reward schemes that maintain their loyalty suit them better than price promotions, which would only give away margin.

**Loyal promotion buyers** (`r n_("Loyal promotion buyers")` households, `r p_(n_("Loyal promotion buyers") / 600)`). This is the most loyal segment, with `r p_(sm("Loyal promotion buyers", "MaxBrShare"))` of volume going to one brand and only `r round(sm("Loyal promotion buyers", "NoBrands"), 1)` brands bought on average. They buy an average amount, about `r v_(sm("Loyal promotion buyers", "TotalVol"))` units, but `r p_(sm("Loyal promotion buyers", "PurOtherPromo"))` of their volume is bought on other promotions, about `r round(sm("Loyal promotion buyers", "PurOtherPromo") / avg("PurOtherPromo"), 1)` times the average of `r p_(avg("PurOtherPromo"))`. Because this segment is loyal and also responds to promotions, promotions on their favourite brand suit them.

**Promo-6 buyers** (`r n_("Promo-6 buyers")` households, `r p_(n_("Promo-6 buyers") / 600)`). These households buy slightly less than average, about `r v_(sm("Promo-6 buyers", "TotalVol"))` units, at an average frequency. They are among the least loyal, with only `r p_(sm("Promo-6 buyers", "MaxBrShare"))` of volume going to their top brand across `r round(sm("Promo-6 buyers", "NoBrands"), 1)` brands, and `r p_(sm("Promo-6 buyers", "PurPromo6"))` of their volume is bought on promotion 6, about `r round(sm("Promo-6 buyers", "PurPromo6") / avg("PurPromo6"), 1)` times the average of `r p_(avg("PurPromo6"))`. Promotion 6 offers timed at different points of the year suit this segment best.
